find: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles
title: The wrath of Achilles
note: The first lines of European literature announce their subject: not a war, but one man's rage.

find: raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son
title: Priam asks for the body of his son
note: The old king of Troy kneels to the man who killed Hector. Homer ends the poem not in triumph but in a shared grief.

find: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero
title: The man who travelled far and wide
note: The opening invocation, and a hero defined by cunning and endurance rather than strength.

find: renowned Ulysses, honour to the Achaean name
title: The song of the Sirens
note: What the Sirens actually offer is not beauty but knowledge — which is why he has to be tied down.

find: Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled
title: Wisdom through suffering
note: The chorus states the law the whole trilogy will test: understanding is paid for in pain.

find: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man
title: Ode to man
note: Sophocles' chorus catalogues everything humanity has mastered, and then the one thing it has not.

find: We women are of all things wretchedest
title: Medea on the lot of women
note: Spoken to the women of Corinth, in a play produced by men for men, in 431 BC.

find: We children of the fountain and the lake
title: The chorus of frogs
note: Dionysus rows across the lake of the dead and is heckled by amphibians. Comedy's oldest surviving running gag.

find: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must
title: The Melian dialogue
note: Athens explains to a small neutral island why justice is not on the table. The island refuses; Athens destroys it.

find: For heroes have the whole earth for their tomb
title: Pericles' funeral oration
note: The most famous speech in Greek history, delivered over the first war dead — and reported by a man who thought the war was a catastrophe.

find: no one of the living might be called happy
title: Solon's warning to Croesus
note: The richest king in the world asks who is the happiest man alive, and does not like the answer. He remembers it on the pyre.

find: the unexamined life is not worth living
title: The unexamined life
note: Socrates, on trial for his life, explains why he will not agree to stop asking questions.

find: Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius
title: The death of Socrates
note: His last words are a reminder about a small debt. Readers have argued about what he meant ever since.

find: Behold! human beings living in a underground den
title: The allegory of the cave
note: Prisoners chained facing a wall have never seen anything but shadows, and would not thank you for the sun.

find: Arms, and the man I sing
title: Arms and the man
note: Virgil opens by naming both halves of his poem: the war of the Iliad and the wandering of the Odyssey.

find: So great the evils to which religion could prompt
title: So great the evils
note: Lucretius' verdict on the sacrifice of Iphigenia, and the line that made him notorious for two thousand years.

find: The die is cast
title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
note: Plutarch's account of the moment a provincial governor became a civil war.

find: Begin the morning by saying to thyself
title: Begin the morning by saying to thyself
note: The emperor's private note to himself about the people he is about to have to deal with.

find: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen
title: Not things, but opinions about things
note: The sentence the whole Stoic programme rests on, from a manual written by a former slave.

find: our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee
title: Our heart is restless
note: The opening of the first autobiography, addressed throughout not to the reader but to God.

find: Give me chastity and continency, only not yet
title: Only not yet
note: Augustine remembers the exact shape of his own reluctance, which is why the book still reads as modern.

find: these two cities are entangled together in this world
title: The two cities
note: Written after Rome fell in 410, to answer Romans who blamed the Christians for it.

find: The existence of God can be proved in five ways
title: The five ways
note: Aquinas' five arguments, stated in the compressed form that made them the standard reference for centuries.
